title: Persistent Homology of the Prime Point Cloud: The Topology of Arithmetic
description: The zero-dimensional persistent homology of the primes, placed at their own values on the real line, is a fully solved topological object whose barcode, Betti curve, merge scale, and total persistence are exact closed-form functions of the prime gaps. In particular the total persistence of the first n primes telescopes to p_n - 2, tying aggregate topological complexity directly to the Prime Number Theorem.
key_results: Bar-length identity: the finite bars of the H0 barcode of the prime point cloud have lengths exactly equal to the prime gaps g_i = p_{i+1} - p_i.
Betti formula: the number of connected components at scale epsilon over the first n primes is b0 = 1 + #{ i < n : g_i > epsilon }.
Global merge scale: the first n primes form a single connected component exactly at and above the largest prime gap max_{i<n} g_i.
Total-persistence identity: the total persistence of the first n primes telescopes to p_n - 2, whose growth is the Prime Number Theorem.
Unboundedness: the barcode contains finite bars of arbitrarily large length, because prime gaps are unbounded.
article:
# The Topology of Arithmetic: Listening to the Shape of the Primes

## A point cloud made of primes

Take the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ... and drop each one onto the number line at its own value: the prime 2 at position 2, the prime 101 at position 101. What you get is a point cloud clumped near the beginning and thinning toward infinity.

A modern branch of mathematics, topological data analysis, exists to extract shape from exactly this kind of scatter. Its central tool, persistent homology, asks: if I blur the points together, at what scales do features appear and disappear? Applied to the primes, this turns the erratic sequence into a clean topological object whose every feature is governed by the gaps between consecutive primes.

## Blurring the dots

Imagine each prime is a bead on a wire, and grow a halo of radius epsilon around every bead. When epsilon is 0 the beads are isolated. As epsilon grows, neighboring halos fuse: consecutive primes p_n and p_{n+1} merge when epsilon reaches g_n = p_{n+1} - p_n, the n-th prime gap. This growing family of shapes is a filtration, and persistent homology tracks how connected components are born and die.

## The barcode

When two components merge, the elder rule says the younger dies and the older survives; the component anchored at 2 lives forever. Every other component is born at scale 0 and dies at the gap to its left, so its lifespan is exactly a prime gap. Collecting all birth-death pairs gives a barcode. The first punchline: the bar lengths of the prime point cloud are exactly the prime gaps.

## Counting pieces

At scale epsilon among the first n primes, the number of components is b0 = 1 + #{ gaps exceeding epsilon }. As epsilon rises this only decreases, dropping by one whenever epsilon crosses a gap value: a descending staircase.

## When everything becomes one

The count drops to 1 exactly when epsilon exceeds the largest gap. This global merge scale is simply the biggest local gap.

## Total persistence

Add up all finite bar lengths. Because they are the gaps g_1, ..., g_{n-1}, the sum telescopes: total persistence equals p_n - 2. All the jagged irregularity washes out, leaving the n-th prime minus the first. By the Prime Number Theorem this grows like n log n, so the Prime Number Theorem reappears as a statement about accumulated topological persistence.

## The bars never stop growing

Prime gaps are unbounded: the run M!+2, ..., M!+M is all composite, so gaps exceed any bound. Hence the barcode contains bars of arbitrarily large length; the topology never settles at any finite scale.

## Why this matters

Persistent homology finds hidden structure in messy data. Turned on the primes it manufactures no spurious structure; it distills them to the gap sequence and re-expresses deep facts of analytic number theory as topological statements. The dictionary runs both ways: the Twin Prime Conjecture is the claim that a bar of length 2 recurs forever, and the Hardy-Littlewood conjectures predict the precise bar-length frequencies.

## Escaping the line

Pairing each prime with the next, p_n -> (p_n, p_{n+1}), lifts the cloud into the plane where it can enclose holes and one-dimensional persistent homology becomes nonempty. Whether those loops encode genuine arithmetic or randomness is open.

## The shape of a mystery

The topological viewpoint offers a new way of seeing: the primes as a growing, merging cloud whose every scale is dictated by its gaps, whose accumulated complexity is exactly p_n - 2, and whose barcode never stops producing longer bars.
research_paper: See RESEARCH_PAPER.md for the full paper. Abstract: We develop the zero-dimensional persistent homology of the point cloud formed by placing the n-th prime p_n at position p_n, filtered by the Vietoris-Rips scale parameter. We prove it is a genuine persistence module whose entire structure is determined by the prime gaps g_n = p_{n+1} - p_n. Main results: (i) the barcode consists of one infinite bar together with finite bars whose lengths are exactly the prime gaps; (ii) b0(epsilon, n) = 1 + #{ i < n : g_i > epsilon }; (iii) the first n primes form a single component precisely at and above the global merge scale max_{i<n} g_i; (iv) total persistence telescopes to p_n - 2; and (v) the barcode contains bars of arbitrarily large length. Together these establish a dictionary between analytic number theory and topological data analysis: the Prime Number Theorem becomes the growth law of total persistence, and the Twin Prime and Hardy-Littlewood conjectures become statements about the multiplicity and frequency of bar lengths.

demos.name: Barcode Reconstruction and the Bar-Length Identity
demos.description: Constructs the zero-dimensional Vietoris-Rips barcode of the first n primes and verifies that the multiset of finite bar lengths is exactly the multiset of prime gaps, alongside the single infinite bar anchored at 2. Demonstrates that the barcode is a faithful re-encoding of the prime-gap sequence.
demos.code:
from typing import List, Tuple


def first_n_primes(n: int) -> List[int]:
    primes: List[int] = []
    c = 2
    while len(primes) < n:
        if all(c % p for p in primes if p * p <= c):
            primes.append(c)
        c += 1
    return primes


def prime_gaps(primes: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    return [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(len(primes) - 1)]


def barcode(primes: List[int]) -> Tuple[List[Tuple[float, float]], Tuple[float, float]]:
    gaps = prime_gaps(primes)
    finite_bars = [(0.0, float(g)) for g in gaps]
    return finite_bars, (0.0, float('inf'))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    primes = first_n_primes(10)
    finite, infinite = barcode(primes)
    lengths = [b[1] - b[0] for b in finite]
    gaps = [float(g) for g in prime_gaps(primes)]
    print('primes      :', primes)
    print('bar lengths :', lengths)
    print('prime gaps  :', gaps)
    print('infinite bar:', infinite)
    print('identity    :', lengths == gaps)

algorithms.name: Zero-Dimensional Prime Barcode Construction via the Elder Rule
algorithms.description: Constructs the H0 persistence barcode of the prime point cloud directly from the gap sequence. Because the points are sorted on a line, connected components are maximal runs of consecutive primes bounded by gaps exceeding the scale; by the elder rule each merge kills the younger component at scale equal to the bounding gap. The algorithm therefore emits one infinite bar for the component of 2 and a finite bar [0, g_i) for each gap g_i. Complexity: O(n) after obtaining the primes; prime sieving in O(N log log N) dominates.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: primes p_1 < ... < p_n
OUTPUT: finite bars F, infinite bar I
1. F <- empty list
2. I <- (0, +infinity)          # component anchored at p_1
3. for i = 1 to n-1:
4.     g_i <- p_{i+1} - p_i      # i-th prime gap
5.     append (0, g_i) to F      # bar of the component rooted at p_{i+1}
6. return (F, I)
algorithms.code:
from typing import List, Tuple


def prime_barcode(primes: List[int]) -> Tuple[List[Tuple[float, float]], Tuple[float, float]]:
    """Return (finite_bars, infinite_bar) for the H0 barcode of the primes."""
    finite_bars: List[Tuple[float, float]] = []
    infinite_bar: Tuple[float, float] = (0.0, float('inf'))
    for i in range(len(primes) - 1):
        gap: int = primes[i + 1] - primes[i]
        finite_bars.append((0.0, float(gap)))
    return finite_bars, infinite_bar

algorithms.name: Betti Curve Sweep and Merge-Scale Detection
algorithms.description: Computes the entire zeroth Betti curve of the first n primes as a right-continuous decreasing step function of the scale epsilon. Sorting the distinct gap values lets the algorithm sweep upward, decrementing the component count as each gap value is crossed, and reports the global merge scale as the largest gap, the scale at which the count first reaches 1. Complexity: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: primes p_1 < ... < p_n
OUTPUT: Betti curve as (epsilon, b0) steps; merge scale M
1. gaps <- [ p_{i+1} - p_i : i = 1..n-1 ]
2. count <- n                        # b0 just above eps = 0
3. curve <- [ (0, n) ]
4. for each distinct value v in sorted(gaps) ascending:
5.     count <- 1 + #{ g in gaps : g > v }
6.     append (v, count) to curve
7. M <- max(gaps)                     # global merge scale
8. return curve, M
algorithms.code:
from typing import List, Tuple


def betti_curve_and_merge(primes: List[int]) -> Tuple[List[Tuple[float, int]], int]:
    """Return the Betti staircase and the global merge scale."""
    gaps: List[int] = [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(len(primes) - 1)]
    curve: List[Tuple[float, int]] = [(0.0, len(primes))]
    for v in sorted(set(gaps)):
        count: int = 1 + sum(1 for g in gaps if g > v)
        curve.append((float(v), count))
    merge_scale: int = max(gaps)
    return curve, merge_scale

algorithms.name: Telescoping Total-Persistence Evaluation
algorithms.description: Evaluates the total persistence of the first n primes. The naive method sums the n-1 finite bar lengths in O(n); the closed form derived from telescoping returns p_n - 2 in O(1) once p_n is known. The algorithm returns both and asserts their equality, providing an internal consistency check of the total-persistence identity.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: primes p_1 < ... < p_n
OUTPUT: total persistence TP
1. naive <- 0
2. for i = 1 to n-1:
3.     naive <- naive + (p_{i+1} - p_i)
4. closed <- p_n - 2               # telescoping identity, p_1 = 2
5. assert naive == closed
6. return closed
algorithms.code:
from typing import List


def total_persistence(primes: List[int]) -> int:
    """Total persistence of the first n primes, checked two ways."""
    naive: int = sum(primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(len(primes) - 1))
    closed: int = primes[-1] - 2
    assert naive == closed, 'telescoping identity violated'
    return closed

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from typing import List


def first_n_primes(n: int) -> List[int]:
    primes: List[int] = []
    c = 2
    while len(primes) < n:
        if all(c % p for p in primes if p * p <= c):
            primes.append(c)
        c += 1
    return primes


def plot_barcode(n: int = 25) -> None:
    primes = first_n_primes(n)
    gaps = [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(n - 1)]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    maxlen = max(gaps) * 1.3
    ax.hlines(0, 0, maxlen, color='crimson', lw=2)
    ax.annotate('', xy=(maxlen, 0), xytext=(maxlen - 1, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='crimson'))
    ax.text(maxlen, 0.2, 'infinite bar (component of 2)', color='crimson')
    for i, g in enumerate(gaps, start=1):
        ax.hlines(i, 0, g, color='steelblue', lw=2)
    ax.set_xlabel('scale epsilon')
    ax.set_ylabel('bar index')
    ax.set_title('H0 barcode of the prime point cloud (bar length = prime gap)')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('prime_barcode.png', dpi=150)
    print('wrote prime_barcode.png')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    plot_barcode(25)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from typing import List


def first_n_primes(n: int) -> List[int]:
    primes: List[int] = []
    c = 2
    while len(primes) < n:
        if all(c % p for p in primes if p * p <= c):
            primes.append(c)
        c += 1
    return primes


def plot_betti(n: int = 50) -> None:
    primes = first_n_primes(n)
    gaps = [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(n - 1)]
    xs = np.linspace(0, max(gaps) + 1, 800)
    ys = [1 + sum(1 for g in gaps if g > eps) for eps in xs]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
    ax.step(xs, ys, where='post', color='darkgreen')
    ax.axvline(max(gaps), ls='--', color='gray', label=f'merge scale = {max(gaps)}')
    ax.set_xlabel('scale epsilon')
    ax.set_ylabel('b0(epsilon, n)')
    ax.set_title(f'Betti staircase for the first {n} primes')
    ax.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('betti_curve.png', dpi=150)
    print('wrote betti_curve.png')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    plot_betti(50)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import math
from typing import List


def first_n_primes(n: int) -> List[int]:
    primes: List[int] = []
    c = 2
    while len(primes) < n:
        if all(c % p for p in primes if p * p <= c):
            primes.append(c)
        c += 1
    return primes


def plot_tp(nmax: int = 3000, step: int = 50) -> None:
    primes = first_n_primes(nmax)
    ns = list(range(step, nmax + 1, step))
    tp = [primes[n - 1] - 2 for n in ns]
    nlogn = [n * math.log(n) for n in ns]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

    ax.plot(ns, nlogn, label='n log n', color='orange', ls='--')
    ax.set_xlabel('n')
    ax.set_ylabel('value')
    ax.set_title('Total persistence and its n log n asymptotic')
    ax.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('total_persistence.png', dpi=150)
    print('wrote total_persistence.png')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    plot_tp(3000, 50)

future_directions:
# Future Directions - The Topology of Arithmetic

This cycle established that the zero-dimensional persistent homology of the prime point cloud is a genuine persistence module whose entire structure - functorial merging, total persistence, global merge scale, unbounded bars, and Betti number - is read off the sequence of prime gaps. The following conjectures push that correspondence further.

## 1. The barcode length distribution follows the Hardy-Littlewood law

**Conjecture.** For each even g, the asymptotic density of H0 bars of death scale exactly g among the first N bars is proportional to the Hardy-Littlewood singular series for gap g; in particular bars of length 2, 4, and 6 occur with the classically predicted relative frequencies, and no even length is ever absent from arbitrarily long windows.

*The key insight is* that a bar of death scale g is exactly a maximal run whose bounding gap equals g, so the bar-length histogram of the barcode is literally the prime-gap histogram, transporting the entire analytic theory of gap distribution into a topological invariant.

*Why now?* The present cycle proved the barcode is unbounded and that its bar lengths are precisely the gaps; the natural next quantitative step is the distribution of those lengths, for which the Hardy-Littlewood conjectures give a sharp, testable target.

## 2. Total persistence grows like n log n

**Conjecture.** The total persistence of the first n bars - proved here to equal p_n - 2 - satisfies p_n - 2 ~ n log n, and more precisely the normalized total persistence (p_n - 2)/(n log n) -> 1.

*The key insight is* that total persistence is not an independent analytic quantity but is identically the n-th prime minus two, so the growth rate of aggregate topological persistence is exactly the prime number theorem in disguise.

*Why now?* With the telescoping identity total_persistence = p_n - 2 in hand, the asymptotics of total persistence reduce to a known and provable statement about p_n, making this the most immediately reachable refinement.

## 3. The Betti curve has a universal staircase profile

**Conjecture.** Viewed as a function of the scale epsilon, the Betti number b0(epsilon, n) = 1 + #{gaps <= n exceeding epsilon} is a right-continuous decreasing step function whose rescaled profile, under epsilon -> epsilon / log p_n, converges to a deterministic limiting curve as n -> infinity.

*The key insight is* that each downward step of the Betti curve is triggered by one prime gap crossing the threshold epsilon, so the shape of the curve is a cumulative count of gaps and its limiting profile encodes the limiting law of normalized prime gaps.

*Why now?* This cycle gave the exact finite-scale formula for b0; converting an exact counting formula into a scaling limit is the standard and now well-motivated continuation.

## 4. Higher-dimensional prime clouds carry genuine loops

**Conjecture.** Placing the primes on a curve in the plane by p_n -> (p_n, p_{n+1}) (consecutive-prime pairs) produces a point cloud in which one-dimensional persistent homology is nontrivial; the resulting loops encode correlations between nearby primes in the spirit of the Hardy-Littlewood conjectures, and their persistence statistics distinguish the prime cloud from a random cloud with the same gap distribution.

modules.demo:
"""
Persistent Homology of the Prime Point Cloud: The Topology of Arithmetic
========================================================================

Numerical demonstrations of the main results.

Place the n-th prime p_n at position p_n on the real line, and grow a
Vietoris-Rips filtration with scale parameter epsilon. The zero-dimensional
persistent homology (connected components) is governed entirely by the prime
gaps g_n = p_{n+1} - p_n. This module verifies:

  (1) Bar-length identity      : finite bar lengths == prime gaps.
  (2) Betti formula            : b0(eps, n) = 1 + #{ gaps g_i > eps , i < n }.
  (3) Global merge scale       : b0 == 1 iff eps >= max gap.
  (4) Total-persistence identity: sum of gaps == p_n - 2  (telescoping).
  (5) Unbounded bars           : prime gaps (hence bars) grow without bound.

Self-contained; standard library only.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from bisect import bisect_right
from typing import List, Tuple


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Prime generation                                                            #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def first_n_primes(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """Return the first ``n`` primes via a growing sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    if n < 1:
        return []
    # Upper bound for the n-th prime (valid for n >= 6); pad for small n.
    import math

    if n < 6:
        limit = 15
    else:
        limit = int(n * (math.log(n) + math.log(math.log(n)))) + 10
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i :: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i :: i]))
    primes = [i for i in range(2, limit + 1) if sieve[i]]
    while len(primes) < n:  # safety net if the bound was too tight
        limit *= 2
        sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
        sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
        for i in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
            if sieve[i]:
                sieve[i * i :: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i :: i]))
        primes = [i for i in range(2, limit + 1) if sieve[i]]
    return primes[:n]


def prime_gaps(primes: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Return the consecutive gaps g_i = p_{i+1} - p_i."""
    return [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(len(primes) - 1)]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Persistent homology quantities                                              #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def barcode(primes: List[int]) -> Tuple[List[Tuple[float, float]], Tuple[float, float]]:
    """H0 barcode of the prime point cloud.

    Returns (finite_bars, infinite_bar) where each finite bar is [0, g_i).
    """
    gaps = prime_gaps(primes)
    finite_bars = [(0.0, float(g)) for g in gaps]
    infinite_bar = (0.0, float("inf"))
    return finite_bars, infinite_bar


def betti0(eps: float, primes: List[int]) -> int:
    """b0(eps, n) = 1 + #{ i < n : g_i > eps }."""
    gaps = prime_gaps(primes)
    return 1 + sum(1 for g in gaps if g > eps)


def global_merge_scale(primes: List[int]) -> int:
    """Smallest scale at which the first n primes form one component."""
    return max(prime_gaps(primes))


def total_persistence(primes: List[int]) -> int:
    """Sum of finite bar lengths (== sum of gaps)."""
    return sum(prime_gaps(primes))


def betti_curve(primes: List[int]) -> List[Tuple[float, int]]:
    """The descending Betti staircase as (eps, b0) at each distinct gap value."""
    gaps = sorted(set(prime_gaps(primes)))
    curve: List[Tuple[float, int]] = [(0.0, len(primes))]
    for g in gaps:
        curve.append((float(g), betti0(float(g), primes)))
    return curve


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstrations                                                              #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def demo_bar_length_identity(n: int = 10) -> None:
    primes = first_n_primes(n)
    finite_bars, _ = barcode(primes)
    lengths = [b[1] - b[0] for b in finite_bars]
    gaps = [float(g) for g in prime_gaps(primes)]
    print("=== (1) Bar-length identity: bar lengths == prime gaps ===")
    print(f"first {n} primes : {primes}")
    print(f"bar lengths      : {lengths}")
    print(f"prime gaps       : {gaps}")
    print(f"identity holds   : {lengths == gaps}\n")


def demo_betti_and_merge(n: int = 10) -> None:
    primes = first_n_primes(n)
    print("=== (2)/(3) Betti formula and global merge scale ===")
    for eps in [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0]:
        print(f"b0(eps={eps:>4}, n={n}) = {betti0(eps, primes)}")
    M = global_merge_scale(primes)
    print(f"global merge scale M_n = max gap = {M}")
    print(f"b0 == 1 at eps = M_n : {betti0(float(M), primes) == 1}")
    print(f"b0  > 1 just below   : {betti0(float(M) - 0.5, primes) > 1}\n")


def demo_total_persistence(sizes: List[int]) -> None:
    print("=== (4) Total-persistence identity: sum of gaps == p_n - 2 ===")
    print(f"{'n':>8} {'total persistence':>20} {'p_n - 2':>12} {'match':>7}")
    for n in sizes:
        primes = first_n_primes(n)
        tp = total_persistence(primes)
        pred = primes[-1] - 2
        print(f"{n:>8} {tp:>20} {pred:>12} {str(tp == pred):>7}")
    print()


def demo_unbounded_bars(n: int = 100000) -> None:
    primes = first_n_primes(n)
    gaps = prime_gaps(primes)
    print("=== (5) Unbounded bars: record gaps (bar lengths) grow ===")
    record = 0
    for i, g in enumerate(gaps):
        if g > record:
            record = g
            print(f"new record bar length {g:>4} between primes "
                  f"{primes[i]} and {primes[i + 1]}")
    print(f"largest bar length among first {n} primes: {max(gaps)}\n")


def demo_asymptotics(sizes: List[int]) -> None:
    import math

    print("=== Corollary: TP(n) / (n log n) -> 1 (Prime Number Theorem) ===")
    print(f"{'n':>8} {'TP(n)':>12} {'n log n':>14} {'ratio':>8}")
    for n in sizes:
        primes = first_n_primes(n)
        tp = total_persistence(primes)
        nlogn = n * math.log(n)
        print(f"{n:>8} {tp:>12} {nlogn:>14.1f} {tp / nlogn:>8.4f}")
    print()
